newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice supports White House Whitewater appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice supports White House Whitewater appeal.

text.p: The Justice Department Friday urged the Supreme Court to hear a White House appeal arguing that notes by its lawyers on talks with first lady Hllary Rodham Clinton be kept from Whitewater prosecutors.
It said a U.S. appeals court was wrong in its ruling that the attorney-client privilege does not apply to the notes subpoenaed by Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr.
But the department refused to embrace the White House position that the attorney-client privilege was absolute and therefore must prevail against a federal grand jury subpoena.

Department lawyers said such disputes normally would be resolved within the government. In cases involving outside independent counsels, a federal judge should weigh the various considerations and decide the dispute, they said.

Lawyers for the White House and Mrs. Clinton say the attorney-client privilege protects the notes. Starr says the lawyers have a duty to turn over the notes and that Mrs. Clinton was not a client of the White House lawyers.

Acting Solicitor General Seth Waxman said the appeals court ruling threatens White House and other government lawyers "with an ever-present potential for unrestrained intrusion into their ongoing attorney-client communications.

"That result would impair the ability of the president and (and the heads of federal agenies) to obtain frank, fully informed and confidential legal advice," said Waxman, a Clinton administration political appointee.
White House lawyers and Whitewater prosecutors recently met with Justice Department officials to press their positions.
The Justice Department's 25-page filing increased the chances, but does not guarantee, that the Supreme Court will hear the case.
The Supreme Court was expected to decide by the end of June whether it will hear the White House appeal. If it denies the appeal, the notes would have to be surrendered.
If the high court grants review, oral arguments would be scheduled during its term that begins in October, and a ruling most likely would be reached late this year or in 1998.

The case even spawned disagreement within the Justice Department, with lawyers from its civil division completely supporting the White House and the criminal division advocating the view that ultimately prevailed.

Starr has been conducting a lengthy investigation into the Whitewater affair, a complex web of Arkansas business deals involving the Clintons, and allegations of a later coverup. President Clinton and his wife have not been accused of any wrongdoing.

At issue are conversations Mrs. Clinton had on July 11, 1995, and Jan. 26, 1996, concerning her role in Whitewater. The notes were taken when Mrs. Clinton was talking with her private Whitewater attorney, David Kendall.

White House lawyers were present at both conversations and took notes. A federal grand jury, acting at Starr's direction, issued a subpoena for the notes a year ago, triggering a legal battle that has ended up at the Supreme Court.

The 1995 notes related to Mrs. Clinton's activities after the suicide of White House lawyer Vince Foster. The 1996 notes related to Mrs. Clinton's testimony about her law firm's billing records outlining work she did for the failing Arkansas savings and loan owned by her Whitewater partner.
